name: Web3 Infrastructure Investor Deck
description: A dark technical fundraising system for explaining Web3 infrastructure through an execution gap, modular architecture, ecosystem value, live network evidence, and a milestone-led raise.
style_guide:
# Web3 Infrastructure Investor Deck

## Design intent

Create a technically credible fundraising deck for protocols, rollup infrastructure, interoperability systems, data-availability services, sequencers, validators, developer platforms, and adjacent Web3 infrastructure. The visual character is a dark operations console made investor-readable: near-black blue surfaces, high-contrast white conclusions, electric green proof points, modular architecture blocks, compact evidence labels, and disciplined horizontal rules.

The deck should explain why a foundational system is needed, how it works, who receives value, what production evidence exists, and how capital advances verifiable milestones. It must not rely on crypto spectacle. The reference previews are for visual-language learning only; do not copy their protocol name, architecture, security claims, transaction volume, customers, token mechanics, team, raise, dates, or roadmap.

## Canvas and grid

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `64–72 px` side margins, `34–42 px` top navigation, and `24–30 px` for sources and page state.
- Use a 12-column grid with `16–18 px` gutters. Snap metric cards, architectural layers, stakeholder modules, charts, and comparison columns to the same grid.
- Reserve `110–145 px` for a small module label, a conclusion-first headline, and a brief supporting statement. Leave the lower field for one dominant technical or commercial exhibit.
- Prefer full-width stacked architecture, three-column stakeholder structures, `8/4` chart-and-metrics splits, and a wide roadmap above a narrow use-of-funds strip.
- Keep panels flat and rectangular. Use `16–22 px` between large modules and `10–14 px` inside compact cards.
- Dense pages must preserve legibility: reduce the number of modules before shrinking text below the specified scale.

## Color system

### Core palette

- Protocol black-blue: `#080A18`. Use for the main canvas and the darkest chart wells.
- Elevated graphite: `#171C2A`. Use for cards, architecture layers, comparison tables, and secondary surfaces.
- Electric protocol green: `#62F45C`. Use for the central mechanism, verified advantage, active milestones, selected values, and key conclusions.
- Signal cyan: `#28C8D8`. Use sparingly for a secondary live metric, data flow, or alternate system state.
- Primary white: `#F4F5F2`. Use for headlines, high-priority labels, and critical values.
- Muted slate: `#8A91A5`. Use for explanations, source notes, inactive roadmap states, and table context.
- Hairline navy: `#293247`. Use for panel borders, chart grids, and separators.

### Semantic use

- Electric green means active, shared, verified, or materially advantaged; it does not automatically mean profitable, secure, or decentralized.
- Cyan means live data, network flow, or a secondary analytical series. Do not let it compete with the green signature.
- Use red or amber only for an explicit exploit, unresolved dependency, risk, or failed threshold and label that meaning in text.
- Maintain WCAG-conscious contrast. Do not set long copy in green or slate on the darkest canvas.

## Typography

- Use `Inter`, `IBM Plex Sans`, `Arial`, or a similar neutral technical sans-serif.
- Use `IBM Plex Mono`, `Roboto Mono`, or another clear monospaced face for addresses, block heights, versions, throughput units, dates, source tags, and benchmark notes.
- Cover title: `48–58 px`, bold. Page headline: `32–40 px`, semibold to bold. Module eyebrow: `9–11 px`, uppercase, tracked. Body copy: `14–17 px`. Tables and architecture detail: `10–13 px`. Sources: `8–10 px`.
- Use white for the sentence structure and green for one decisive phrase or value. Avoid coloring several unrelated phrases in a single headline.
- Keep protocol vocabulary exact. Do not use stylized casing that makes technical names or units ambiguous.

## Components

- Cards use graphite fills, `1 px` navy or green borders, square corners, and no shadow. A card may receive a thin green left rule when it contains the principal proof point.
- Metric cards contain a scope label, a large number, unit and period, plus one sentence explaining provenance or implication.
- Use narrow terminal-like eyebrow labels prefixed by module, layer, signal, or status language, but avoid decorative code that has no informational purpose.
- Architecture layers should be horizontally aligned, ordered, and numbered. Each layer needs responsibility, dependency, and trust or verification boundary.
- Comparison tables use quiet graphite rows and green text only for supported advantages. Competitor cells should remain neutral and factual.
- Footers should carry source, measurement period, network or environment, sample status, and page count.

## Charts and diagrams

- Favor modular layer diagrams, value-flow maps, transaction or usage time series, network KPI clusters, capability comparison tables, milestone roadmaps, and proportional use-of-funds bars.
- Architecture diagrams must identify components controlled by the project, third parties, base chains, off-chain actors, and external trust assumptions.
- Flow arrows should have one consistent direction and visual grammar. Label assets, messages, proofs, fees, or state transitions directly.
- Usage charts must define mainnet, testnet, sandbox, routed, settled, active, unique, annualized, and cumulative terms where relevant.
- Show throughput, latency, finality, availability, validator count, geographic distribution, or security thresholds only when the measurement method is available.
- Avoid token-price charts unless token economics is genuinely in scope and sourced. Never use 3D nodes or decorative network webs as substitutes for architecture.

## Composition families

### Technical cover

Use a near-black canvas, a large left-aligned title with one electric-green phrase, a concise category statement, and a restrained generative network or node image occupying the opposite half. Keep version, confidentiality, presenter, and date compact.

### Infrastructure gap

State the scaling or execution bottleneck in one sentence. Support it with three scoped evidence cards and a full-width opportunity statement. Separate observed ecosystem data from the venture's addressable opportunity.

### Modular architecture

Stack protocol layers vertically and reserve a side panel for the key mechanism, trust model, consensus or proving approach, throughput context, and finality assumptions. Make external dependencies visible.

### Ecosystem value

Use three aligned stakeholder panels such as developers, users, and ecosystem operators. Explain action, received value, incentive, and measurable outcome for each. Do not mistake feature lists for a value loop.

### Business model and network evidence

Pair revenue mechanisms with a usage time series, a compact KPI grid, and a capability comparison. Clarify current revenue, annualized run rate, contracted revenue, grants, and projected monetization.

### Team, roadmap, and use of funds

Show only role-relevant team evidence. Connect the raise to a milestone roadmap and a proportional capital allocation. Every milestone needs a measurable completion condition, dependency, and expected timing.

## Imagery

- Use abstract node networks, protocol topology, data-flow particles, terminal grids, or restrained chain geometry with licensed or generated provenance.
- Keep imagery on the cover or in section dividers. Analytical pages should be diagram- and evidence-led.
- Use one thin-line icon family for developer, user, validator, network, security, and governance concepts.
- Avoid coins, rockets, astronauts, neon cityscapes, anonymous hoodie imagery, trading screens, speculative price motifs, and generic blockchain cubes.

## Content integrity

- Do not invent transactions, total value locked, wallets, validators, commits, customers, chains, rollups, revenue, fees, uptime, throughput, latency, finality, exploit losses, market size, or competitive claims.
- State network and environment for every metric: mainnet, testnet, devnet, simulation, or combined. Define period, counting method, deduplication, and source.
- Separate deployed code, audited code, production usage, pilots, integrations, signed commitments, grant-funded work, and roadmap items.
- Security language must name the threat model, trust assumptions, audit scope, auditor, date, unresolved findings, and whether a claim is tested or theoretical.
- Do not claim trustlessness, decentralization, atomicity, interoperability, censorship resistance, or shared security without precise technical support.
- Identify whether revenue is realized, contracted, protocol-generated, foundation-funded, token-denominated, annualized, or projected.
- Missing evidence should be omitted or labeled `hypothesis`, `target`, `simulation`, `testnet`, `planned`, or `to be verified`. Do not create numbers to make the dashboard look complete.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview protocol names, architecture labels, technical mechanisms, metrics, exploits, competitors, raise amount, team identities, roadmap, or contact details.
- Do not use electric green as decoration on every border, icon, and paragraph; reserve it for hierarchy and meaning.
- Do not conceal external trust, centralization, admin-key, data-availability, bridge, oracle, sequencer, governance, or upgrade risks.
- Do not compare unlike systems without matching scope, version, network, and measurement period.
- Do not use a token as evidence of product-market fit or confuse transaction count with retained users or revenue.
- Do not use glassmorphism, heavy gradients, glowing card shadows, rounded consumer-app panels, 3D charts, or illegible code backgrounds.
- Do not reduce the raise to a percentage bar without milestone ownership and measurable outcomes.
